request_debug.prompt_preview:
You write per-candidate post-mortems for a slopmortem pipeline. Given a fresh pitch and one dead-startup canonical document, produce a single LLMSynthesis JSON object that explains why this dead startup is similar, where the new pitch could diverge, what killed the dead startup, and what the new founder should learn.

Rules:
- Ground every claim in the candidate document or in tool calls. Do not invent facts.
- A `Trusted facts` block (typed pipeline data — not user input) appears below the pitc

response.text: {"candidate_id":"knewton::edtech","name":"Knewton","one_liner":"Adaptive learning SaaS platform that personalized educational content for publishers, schools, and developers in higher education and K-12.","similarity":{"business_model":{"score":4,"rationale":"Both are B2B SaaS platforms licensed to institutional customers (Knewton to publishers and universities; the pitch to academic spinouts and small CROs). Both use subscription-recurring monetization. However, the vertical, workflow, and underlying IP are entirely different — edtech vs. biotech lab management — reducing practical business-model overlap despite the structural similarity."},"market":{"score":2,"rationale":"Knewton served the educational publishing and higher-education market; the pitch targets academic spinouts and small contract research organizations in the life sciences. These are distinct markets with different regulatory environments, buyer dynamics, and competitive landscapes. Overlap is limited to the shared pattern of selling into resource-constrained, mission-driven institutions."},"gtm":{"score":3,"rationale":"Both relied on enterprise-style partnerships and licensing deals with incumbent institutions. Knewton's GTM was anchored in deals with major publishers (Pearson, HMH, Macmillan). The pitch's GTM would similarly depend on landing early academic or CRO partners. The channel and relationship-driven nature is analogous, though the pitch targets far smaller, more fragmented customers."},"stage_scale":{"score":5,"rationale":"Knewton raised over $157M across six rounds before a distressed acquisition for under $17M. The pitch is presumably at an early stage. The scale trajectories are very different, but Knewton's journey illustrates the dangers of over-capitalizing a B2B SaaS platform before achieving sustainable unit economics — a cautionary scale story relevant to any early-stage B2B SaaS founder."}},"why_similar":"Both Knewton and the pitch are B2B SaaS platforms licensed to institutional buyers using a subscription-recurring model. Both attempt to deliver specialized workflow intelligence to customers (students/educators vs. lab scientists) within large, tradition-bound institutions (universities/publishers vs. academic spinouts/CROs). Knewton's core challenge — convincing institutional buyers to replace entrenched workflows with a new software layer — mirrors the adoption challenge the pitch will face in getting small CROs and academic spinouts to adopt a centralized assay-management platform.","where_diverged":"1. Vertical: Knewton was edtech (adaptive learning); the pitch is biotech/life sciences (wet-lab assay management) — fundamentally different regulatory, compliance, and workflow contexts. 2. Customer size and fragmentation: Knewton targeted large publishers and universities; the pitch explicitly targets small CROs and academic spinouts, a far more fragmented and resource-constrained customer base with different procurement cycles. 3. Product depth: Knewton's platform consumed and re-served digital content; the pitch involves wet-lab instrumentation data and experimental protocol management, which may require deeper integrations with lab hardware and compliance standards (e.g., 21 CFR Part 11). 4. Capital intensity: Knewton raised ~$157M and was acquired for under $17M; the pitch is presumably early-stage and can potentially pursue a leaner path.","failure_causes":["over-capitalization relative to achievable market size","partnership dependency on large publishers who controlled content and distribution","inability to demonstrate clear, measurable ROI to institutional buyers at scale","commoditization of adaptive learning features by larger edtech incumbents","distressed acquisition below total capital raised indicating value destruction","failure to achieve sustainable unit economics before scaling"],"lessons_for_input":["Validate willingness-to-pay with small CROs before raising large rounds — Knewton raised $157M into a market that could not absorb its valuation","Avoid over-reliance on a single large partner or channel; diversify your customer base from day one","Ensure your platform integrates tightly with existing lab workflows and instruments so switching costs protect retention","Define and track a clear ROI metric (e.g., time-to-result, error rate reduction) that you can show to every prospective customer","Keep burn lean at early stages; a distressed acquisition at under $17M on $157M raised is the failure mode to avoid"]}
